evidence:
# Exact tests of two terminal-game closures

Status: self-contained UNVERIFIED candidate counterexamples. No verifier request
is allocated. Only fact 1252b8823bb5a290 is used as a mathematical predecessor;
the new minimax candidate 40601f4c6f496ab8 is not a premise.

## 1. Three anchors are necessary even after optimizing the final step

The claim tested here is that, for every legal fixed prefix, its exact optimized
terminal potential can be evaluated with a mixture supported on at most TWO
prefix anchors, counting the optimum anchor. This claim is false already for
one queried GD step in dimension three. The example keeps both orientations of
every queried-prefix interpolation constraint.

Work with L=1 in R^3. Use the optimum jet (0,0,0), the positive first step
h_0=2, and the following prefix:

    x_0=(8,9,3),  g_0=(0,2,1),  f_0=19/2,
    x_1=(8,5,1),  g_1=(1,0,0),  f_1=11/2.

Thus x_1=x_0-2g_0 and ||x_0||^2=154. The proximal points and offsets are

    y_0=x_0-g_0=(8,7,2),    delta_0=f_0-||g_0||^2/2=7,
    y_1=x_1-g_1=(7,5,1),    delta_1=f_1-||g_1||^2/2=5.

Using the signed Q from the predecessor, ALL six prefix residuals are

    Q_(0,star)=-9,   Q_(star,0)=-7,
    Q_(1,star)=-2,   Q_(star,1)=-5,
    Q_(0,1)=-3,      Q_(1,0)=-1.                         (1)

For example the identity Q_ij=delta_i-delta_j+<g_i,y_j-y_i>
gives Q_(0,1)=2-<(0,2,1),(1,2,1)>=-3. Hence the predecessor constructs
the pointwise maximal legal prefix interpolant as the conjugate of

    H(v)=||v||^2/2+
             max{0, <(8,7,2),v>-7, <(7,5,1),v>-5}.       (2)

Call it F. It is one fixed everywhere-finite convex differentiable 1-smooth
function, with minimum F(0)=0, and it interpolates exactly the jets in (1).
For any nonnegative final step b, its terminal point is

    x_2(b)=(8-b,5,1).

Put v_*=(0,1,0). All three affine planes inside the maximum in (2) are
zero at v_*. Thus H(v_*)=1/2, and the conjugate definition gives

    F(x_2(b)) >= <x_2(b),v_*>-H(v_*)=9/2
                         for EVERY b>=0.                   (3)

At b=3, let alpha_star=alpha_0=alpha_1=1/3. The weighted affine bound on
H and completion of a square give

    F(x_2(3))
      <= (7+5)/3 + (1/2)||x_2(3)-(y_0+y_1)/3||^2
       =4+(1/2)||(0,1,0)||^2=9/2.                         (4)

Consequently the exact final-line-search value of this legal fixed prefix is

    min_(b>=0) 2F(x_2(b))/||x_0||^2 = 9/154.               (5)

The minimizing step and mixture are UNIQUE, and all three weights are
strictly positive. Here are two direct ways to check the asserted necessity.

First, equality in (3) makes v_* the unique conjugate maximizer. The
subgradient condition for (2) then requires

    x_2(b)-v_* = alpha_0 y_0+alpha_1 y_1,
    alpha_0,alpha_1>=0,  alpha_0+alpha_1<=1.               (6)

The subgradient condition follows by separating from the convex hull of
the active plane slopes: a point outside that hull gives a direction in
which <x,v>-H(v) increases. Thus it uses only the finite maximum in (2).
The third and second coordinates of (6) read

    2alpha_0+alpha_1=1,
    7alpha_0+5alpha_1=4.

Their unique solution is alpha_0=alpha_1=1/3. The first coordinate then
gives b=3. The remaining weight on the optimum is 1/3 as well.

Second, the full quadratic mixture expression can be checked directly:

    J(b,alpha_0,alpha_1)
      =2(7alpha_0+5alpha_1)
        +(8-b-8alpha_0-7alpha_1)^2
        +(5-7alpha_0-5alpha_1)^2
        +(1-2alpha_0-alpha_1)^2.                          (7)

It is the upper bound on 2F supplied by the weighted conjugate quadratics.
At (b,alpha_0,alpha_1)=(3,1/3,1/3), its value is 9 and all three derivatives
are zero. Its Hessian is positive definite because the three vectors
g_1,y_0,y_1 are independent; their determinant has absolute value three.
Thus the minimizer of (7) on b>=0 and the simplex is unique. Equations
(3)-(4) show that this bound is exact at the minimizing point, independently
of any general hull or minimax theorem.

## 2. Exact loss from using at most two anchors

The failure has an explicit quantitative size. For every feasible mixture,
the best b in (7) is

    b=8-8alpha_0-7alpha_1>=0.

After optimizing it, set

    Y=(7alpha_0+5alpha_1, 2alpha_0+alpha_1).

The remaining expression is precisely

    9+||Y-(4,1)||^2.                                    (8)

The simplex maps bijectively to the triangle with vertices
O=(0,0), A=(7,2), B=(5,1), and the unconstrained target (4,1) has the
three barycentric weights 1/3. A support of size at most two places Y on
the boundary of this triangle. Its distances to the three edges are:

* To [O,A], squared distance 1/53. The projection coefficient is 30/53,
  lying strictly between zero and one; the determinant is 4*2-1*7=1.
* To [O,B], squared distance 1/26. The projection coefficient is 21/26;
  the determinant is 4*1-1*5=-1.
* To [B,A], the projection coefficient from B is -2/5, so the nearest
  point of that segment is B and the squared distance is one.

Therefore optimizing BOTH the last step and all mixtures of support at
most two gives J=9+1/53, strictly larger than its exact value 9. In the
original normalized objective this is

    9/154 + 1/8162,                                     (9)

whereas the true value is 9/154. No count of active anchors in this
example is inferred from a numerical solution.

This refutes a universal two-anchor formula for the fixed-prefix terminal
game even when the final step is optimized. It does NOT assert that this
particular prefix maximizes the full PEP at h=(2,3), and it does NOT refute
the distinct, unproved statement that some globally worst prefix always
admits a smaller terminal support. The full selected certificate of an
entire PEP is also a different object from the fixed-prefix alpha here.

## 3. The whole schedule value is not jointly convex

For EVERY nonnegative schedule all of whose steps satisfy h_t>=2,

    W_n(h)=product_t(h_t-1)^2.                            (10)

Here is a complete elementary proof. Normalize L=1 and the minimizer to
zero. Adding the two interpolation inequalities between x and zero gives
<x,g>>=||g||^2, and smoothness gives ||g||<=||x||. Thus for h>=2,

    ||x-hg||^2
      =||x||^2-2h<x,g>+h^2||g||^2
      <=||x||^2+h(h-2)||g||^2
      <=(h-1)^2||x||^2.

Iterate this inequality and use 2f(x_n)<=||x_n||^2. This proves the upper
bound in (10) in every finite dimension. The scalar function f(x)=x^2/2
starting at x_0=1 has exactly that normalized error, proving equality.

In particular

    W_2(2,4)=W_2(4,2)=9,
    W_2(3,3)=16 > (9+9)/2.                              (11)

Thus the exact unrestricted value is not jointly convex in all step
coordinates, even on strictly positive schedules. This is a value-level
obstruction, stronger than exhibiting a nonconvex response on one fixed
function. It prevents replacing the proven final-step convexity by an
unqualified joint-convexity argument for all earlier steps. It does not
by itself disprove every possible all-step minimax identity.

## 4. Scope for continued proof search

The three-anchor obstruction is inside the full smooth-convex prefix class
and uses a finite, explicit legal function. It is not caused by dropping
incoming queried-prefix inequalities; every such inequality is strictly
satisfied in (1). It shows that any terminal state compression must retain
enough geometry to represent this triangle after projection along the
last gradient. One scalar value and an assumed pair of active anchors
cannot reproduce the fixed-prefix game.

The current global two-step calibration in finding 81a9c03cf73670f3 remains
separate and unverified: its unavoidable adjacent forward multiplier rules
out universal triangular certificate re-selection. Nothing in the present
example contradicts it or removes that edge. No new claim about remote
forward edges, global Huber tightness, or the asymptotic exact profile is made.

Targeted memory/fact searches found no existing version of (1)-(9). The
Matlas query returned unrelated general convexity statements; no external
result is used. This is the already audited finite conjugate-quadratic
regime of the accepted terminal fact, so no new literature layer is needed
to construct or evaluate these explicit examples.

# An exact overlapping-return episode and its embedding obstruction

Status: unverified counterexample to a proposed LOCAL extension of the
plateau-rank argument. This is not a benchmark-scale construction for H_m.
The last section identifies an explicit obstruction to inserting this same
episode after the preceding low-level pair in H_m.

## 1. Fixed legal function and exact trajectory

Set c=13/5, a=c^(-17), b_j=a c^j, H_0=(), and
H_(j+1)=(H_j,b_j,H_j). Choose r>=22, and let

    b=b_r,  S=sum H_r=a(c^r-2^r)/(c-2),
    lambda=1/(3b),
    P_aff=product_{h in H_r}(1-lambda h),
    v=(b-1)/(S+1).

Equivalently, with lambda held fixed throughout, define P_0=1 and
P_(j+1)=P_j^2(1-lambda b_j); then P_aff=P_r. This is an exact analytic
product recurrence, not a numerical trajectory calculation.

Here b>=c^5=118.81376>100, every factor defining P_aff lies in (0,1), and
S/b is between eta=13/8 and 5/3. Define the positive and negative derivative
magnitudes of one fixed function by

    g_+(R)=R                      for 0<=R<=1,
    g_+(R)=1+lambda(R-1)          for R>=1,
    g_-(R)=min(R,v)              for R>=0.

The derivative is g_+(x) on the positive ray and -g_-(-x) on the negative
ray. It is continuous, nondecreasing and 1-Lipschitz; across zero use
g_+(R)+g_-(T)<=R+T. Its integral f is convex and 1-smooth, with minimum
f(0)=0. All complete function-value areas are

    f(R)=R^2/2                                      for 0<=R<=1,
    f(R)=1/2+(R-1)+lambda(R-1)^2/2                    for R>=1,
    f(-R)=R^2/2                                     for 0<=R<=v,
    f(-R)=vR-v^2/2                                  for R>=v.  (1)

Start at

    X=1+3b(P_aff^(-1)-1).

Consider the exact consecutive blocks and checkpoints

    K_r=(H_r,b,H_r,b c^2,H_r,b).                           (2)

On the affine positive piece, a step h multiplies the gradient by
1-lambda h. Thus the first H_r goes from X to 1. All its intermediate
radii are at least 1 because its initial gradient is P_aff^(-1) and all partial
products are at least P_aff. The low checkpoint b then lands at -(b-1).
The next H_r has constant gradient -v and goes from -(S+1)v to -v.
The checkpoint b c^2 lands at

    Y=(b c^2-1)v.

Define

    z=P_aff[1+(Y-1)/(3b)],
    Z=1+3b(z-1).                                         (3)

The estimates below prove 1<z<3/2-1/(2b). Consequently the third H_r
stays in the same affine positive piece and sends Y to Z. The final
checkpoint b strictly changes sign, landing at

    -B,    B=bz-Z=b(3-2z)-1>0.                           (4)

This is one actual function and one initial point for the entire episode.
No gradient or knot is selected again at an intermediate time.

## 2. Exact bounds proving overlap and the increased endpoint gradient

Put alpha_h=lambda h for the steps of H_r. Then 0<=alpha_h<1 and
sum alpha_h=lambda S<=5/9. Induction in the finite product gives

    P_aff=product(1-alpha_h)>=1-sum alpha_h>=4/9.              (5)

Also log(1-t)<=-t for 0<=t<1 gives
P_aff<=exp(-lambda S)<=exp(-13/24)<3/5. The last strict inequality follows
already from exp(13/24)>=1+13/24+(13/24)^2/2>5/3.

Since b>100,

    Y/b >= [(27/4)(99/100)]/(503/300)
          =8019/2012 >39/10.

Here b c^2-1>=(27/4)b, b-1>=(99/100)b, and
S+1<=(503/300)b were used. Therefore

    z>=(4/9)[1+(39/10-1/100)/3]=689/675>1.                (6)

On the other hand Y/b<c^2/eta=1352/325, hence

    z<(3/5)[1+c^2/(3eta)]=2327/1625.

Since 2327/1625<299/200 and 3/2-1/(2b)>299/200,
the sign-change condition in (4) follows. In particular the positive
endpoint gradient has INCREASED from 1 to z>1 across checkpoint levels
(0,2), even though both positive blocks and the intervening negative block
stay on their assigned rays.

The two positive traversed intervals overlap strictly:

    1<Z<X<Y.                                             (7)

To prove Z<X, compare z with P_aff^(-1). Using P_aff<3/5 gives

    P_aff z=P_aff^2[1+(Y-1)/(3b)]
         <(9/25)[1+c^2/(3eta)]<1.

For the final strict inequality, the bracket is 2327/975, and
(9/25)(2327/975)=20943/24375<1. The inequality X<Y follows from z>1
and the strictly increasing affine H_r map, which sends X to 1 and Y to Z.
Thus the old interval [1,X] and the return interval [Z,Y] have the genuine
overlap [Z,X]. Their gradients are not constant; they are restrictions of
the very same affine derivative, so all overlap data agree automatically.

At the positive return endpoint the exact normalized value is

    2f(Z)/X^2
      = [1+3b(z^2-1)]/[1+3b(P_aff^(-1)-1)]^2.                (8)

At the end of (2), use (4) in the negative-ray formula (1): the normalized
value is B^2/X^2 if B<=v, and (2vB-v^2)/X^2 if B>=v. These are complete
areas, not squared-gradient surrogates. The episode is finite and these
formulas do not establish a comparison to the exact benchmark on H_m.

## 3. Precisely what local assertion fails

With a flat positive H_r block of derivative u, its traversed interval has
length S u. Canonical intervals belonging to different derivative heights
are disjoint, forcing multiplicative separation of their outer radii.
For varying gradients the natural interval of length S u at the endpoint
need not be a constant-gradient interval and need not be disjoint from
the corresponding interval of another endpoint value.

The local claim that the endpoint-gradient rank cannot increase across a
pair of checkpoint levels (0,2), without the flat-block hypothesis, is
therefore false. The legal episode above has endpoint values 1<z and a
rank increase in the finite set {1,z}. Its explicit overlapping interval
(7) identifies the missing hypothesis. This does not refute a possible
global all-scalar bound for H_m: the ordering of neighboring checkpoint
pairs may impose additional restrictions not present in a single episode.

## 4. This exact seed cannot be inserted after the preceding (0,1) pair

The checkpoint substring (0,2,0) occurs in the ruler word for H_(r+3),
but its first positive block is preceded by a pair (0,1). Merely matching
the local substring is not an embedding proof.

For this fixed g_+, the largest negative landing radius at ANY positive
low checkpoint b is b-1. Indeed b g_+(R)-R=(b-1)R on [0,1], while on
[1,infinity) its slope is b lambda-1=-2/3. Its maximum is at R=1.

Suppose the following negative H_r stays negative, as required by the
coarse relay under test. Starting at B_0<=b-1=(S+1)v, it ends at a radius
at most v. If it ever reaches radius at most v, this follows from its
assumed same-sign motion. If it always stays above v, its constant
gradient v makes its terminal radius B_0-Sv<=v, with the same conclusion.
Its terminal gradient magnitude is thus at most v.

The next checkpoint of level 1 can therefore land at positive radius at
most

    (b c-1)v < (c/eta)b=(8/5)b.

But the required initial radius of the episode is

    X=1+3b(P_aff^(-1)-1)>1+2b,

because P_aff<3/5. Hence no such preceding pair (0,1), with its negative
ordinary block staying on that ray, can supply X to this episode.

The concrete failure is an interface mismatch in initial radius, not
illegal local interpolation or a missing function-value area. A recursive
construction would need to modify the inner radial geometry, allow a new
internal crossing pattern, or build a different incoming state. The
displayed fixed function and local episode alone do not solve that task.

claim: Prefix length AND total sum do not determine even the optimized final-stage worst case: for k>=1 and S=2k, rho_last(2,...,2)<=1/4 but rho_last(S,0,...,0)>=S^(2/3)/12, giving an unbounded separation between equal-length/equal-sum prefixes.
evidence:
## 5. Even length and total sum together do not determine the final-stage value

This is a separate, quantitative obstruction to a sum-only state. For a fixed
prefix h_pre of length k define directly

    rho_last(h_pre)=inf_(b>=0) W_(k+1)(h_pre,b).

For every integer k>=1 let S=2k, and compare the two legal prefixes

    h_even=(2,...,2),             k entries,
    h_burst=(S,0,...,0),          k entries.

They have the SAME length and the SAME total sum. Nevertheless

    rho_last(h_even)<=1/4,
    rho_last(h_burst)>=S^(2/3)/12.                       (12)

In particular their values are different for k>=3 and have an unbounded
separation as k increases. This refutes an exact value closure depending
only on (k,S), not merely a claim about one selected function.

For the first upper bound, the norm calculation in Section3 with h=2 gives
||x_k-x_star||<=||x_0-x_star|| for every legal function. Append b=3/2.
At that final stage write x=x_k-x_star, z=grad f(x_k)/L and w for the next
normalized gradient, and use values divided by L and shifted by f_star.
The normalized one-step identity, with the signed Q on samples 0,1,star,
is

    (1/4)||x||^2-2f_1+Q_(0,star)+Q_(1,star)+Q_(1,0)
                      =||(1/2)x-z-w||^2.

Expanding Q and the recursion x_1=x-(3/2)z verifies every term. Since all
Q<=0, it bounds the last objective by (1/4)||x||^2 in the W normalization.
The initial norm bound proves rho_last(h_even)<=1/4 in all dimensions.

For the second lower bound use the verified single-cut fact b98bb807d514e80d,
whose full statement and proof have been read. Its cut at the first step S
and its cut at the appended final step b yield, for EVERY b>=0,

    W_(k+1)(h_burst,b)
       >=max{(S-1)^2/(1+2b), (b-1)_+^2/(S+1)^2}.        (13)

The internal zero steps change neither prefix nor suffix sums in that fact.
If b<=S^(4/3), then S>=2 and the first term in (13) is at least

    (S^2/4)/(1+2S^(4/3)) >= S^(2/3)/12.

If b>S^(4/3), then b>2, b-1>=b/2 and S+1<=3S/2. The second term is
therefore at least

    (b^2/4)/[(3S/2)^2] > S^(2/3)/9.

Taking the infimum over b proves the second part of (12). No compactness
or attainment assertion for this infimum is needed for either bound.

The explicit prefix-sum guard in research/prefix_sum_terminal_guard.md
accordingly supplies a universal LOWER boundary condition q_S, not an exact
schedule-level state variable. The proof of (12) does not use that new,
unverified guard or the unverified minimax result.

author: max4
claim: Candidate exact two-dimensional counterexample refutes the outstanding eight-step primitive seed29a1f4a5269032b1. More generally ANY primitive two-bridge join (a,1+r_L,b,1+r_R,c), without quadratic-balance assumptions, must satisfy r_L r_R[A^2+r_L(T_tot+A)]<=A^2 BC. At a saturated first cut r_L T_tot=A D_tail this forces r_R D_tail<=BC; retained signed moments cannot repair an actual inner-cut defect while that cut stays saturated.
evidence:
# A two-dimensional obstruction at a saturated primitive cut

Status: complete candidate proof, NOT verifier-accepted. No solver or verifier
call. The only existing fact used is 1252b8823bb5a290, for its explicit finite
smooth-convex interpolation construction. Every other identity is proved here.

## 1. Definitions and an energy identity

For a nonnegative physical schedule h of length n let T_tot=1+sum_i h_i.
For normalized smoothness 1 and an optimum jet (0,0,0), put

    Q_ij=f_i-f_j+<g_i,x_j-x_i>+||g_i-g_j||^2/2,
    V_h=2 sum_(i<n) h_i(f_i-f_n)
          +sum_(i<n) h_i(1-h_i)||g_i||^2
          -T_tot(T_tot-1)||g_n||^2.

Here primitive validity means V_h>=0 on every legal convex 1-smooth GD
trajectory. Suppose the sampled data additionally satisfy

    f_i=<g_i,x_i>-||g_i||^2/2 for every i,
    x_n=g_n.

The first condition is exactly Q_(i,star)=0; the second gives
f_n=||g_n||^2/2. Expanding

    ||x_0||^2-||x_n||^2
       =2 sum h_i<g_i,x_i>-sum h_i^2||g_i||^2

therefore gives the exact identity

    V_h=||x_0||^2-T_tot^2||g_n||^2.                 (1)

For any such data, whether or not yet jointly interpolable, write y_i=x_i-g_i.
Direct substitution also gives

    Q_ij=<g_i-g_j,y_j>.                             (2)

## 2. General two-bridge construction

Let a,b,c be arbitrary finite nonnegative blocks, with capacities

    A=1+sum a_i, B=1+sum b_i, C=1+sum c_i.

Take r_L,r_R>0 and h=(a,1+r_L,b,1+r_R,c). Define

    D_tail=B+C+r_R, T_tot=A+D_tail+r_L,
    eta_cut=r_L/D_tail, beta_inner=r_R/C,
    p_aux=-B/r_L.

The first scalar array is a legal Huber trajectory: start at A and use
derivative clip(x,-eta_cut,1). During a and at its endpoint the gradient is
1. Its endpoint is 1. The first bridge lands at -r_L=-eta_cut D_tail.
Every remaining query has gradient -eta_cut, and the final point is
-eta_cut. All the data satisfy the hypotheses of (1), so

    V_base=A^2-T_tot^2 eta_cut^2.                   (3)

The second scalar array is defined as follows. During a use constant
gradient p_aux, start at A p_aux, and end at p_aux. The first bridge lands
at -r_L p_aux=B. On the remaining schedule (b,1+r_R,c) use the ACTUAL
Huber trajectory with derivative clip(x,-beta_inner,1), starting at B.
The b block ends at 1, the second bridge lands at -r_R=-C beta_inner,
and c ends at -beta_inner. Assign every value by
f_i=g_i x_i-g_i^2/2. Thus (1) yields

    V_aux=A^2 B^2/r_L^2-T_tot^2 beta_inner^2.        (4)

The second array is generally NOT interpolable across the first bridge.
It is only auxiliary data; its possible violations are accounted for below.

For epsilon_mix>0, combine both arrays into two-dimensional data

    X_i=(x_i^base,sqrt(epsilon_mix) x_i^aux),
    G_i=(g_i^base,sqrt(epsilon_mix) g_i^aux),
    F_i=f_i^base+epsilon_mix f_i^aux.

The GD equations hold coordinate by coordinate, all Q_(i,star) remain zero,
and X_n=G_n. Consequently

    V_mix=V_base+epsilon_mix V_aux.                 (5)

Here is a complete interpolation audit. Partition the samples into L (a
and its endpoint), M (b and its endpoint after the first bridge), and R (c
and its final endpoint after the second bridge). Overlaps are assigned to
the group whose gradient is used at the relevant bridge. The groups are
disjoint in original time: L includes the first bridge query, M includes
the second bridge query, and R includes the terminal sample.

* Within L all gradients in each scalar array agree, so Q=0.
* Within M union R the auxiliary data are one legal Huber trajectory;
  the base gradients agree, so all Q<=0 there.
* From L to M, the auxiliary target has y_j>=0 and the source gradient
  p_aux<1, so Q_aux<=0. From M to L, the auxiliary target y_i is a
  nonnegative multiple of p_aux<0 and 1-p_aux>0, so Q_aux<=0.
* From L to R, if R_j is the remaining sum of physical c steps after its
  target sample j, the two residuals are

      Q_base=-(1+eta_cut)eta_cut R_j,
      Q_aux=beta_inner(-p_aux-beta_inner)R_j.

* From R to L, if H_i is the remaining sum of physical a steps after its
  target sample i, then

      Q_base=-(1+eta_cut)H_i,
      Q_aux=(-beta_inner-p_aux)p_aux H_i.

Zero remaining sums give zero in both arrays. Thus duplicate positions
caused by zero steps do not require a separate limiting argument.

The optimum-outgoing inequalities hold too: Q_(star,i)=-<G_i,Y_i>,
and the inner product is nonnegative separately in each scalar array.
For the auxiliary L data this is H_i p_aux^2>=0, and in the other groups
it follows directly from their plateau coordinates. Q_(i,star)=0 already.

When r_L r_R<BC, one has -p_aux>beta_inner. The ONLY potentially positive
auxiliary residuals are L-to-R, and all interpolation inequalities hold for

    0<epsilon_mix<=epsilon_max,
    epsilon_max=eta_cut(1+eta_cut)
                    /[beta_inner(-p_aux-beta_inner)].             (6)

When r_L r_R>BC the ONLY potentially positive auxiliary residuals are
R-to-L, and all inequalities hold for

    0<epsilon_mix<=epsilon_max,
    epsilon_max=(1+eta_cut)
                    /[(-p_aux)(beta_inner+p_aux)].                 (7)

When r_L r_R=BC both cross families are nonpositive for any epsilon_mix.

All these are complete original-index interpolation checks, including both
cross directions and both optimum directions.

## 3. One fixed globally legal function

Include the zero optimum sample and define, on R^2,

    H_mix(v)=max_i { c_i+<X_i,v-G_i>+||v-G_i||^2/2 },
    c_i=<G_i,X_i>-F_i=||G_i||^2/2,
    f_mix(x)=sup_v { <x,v>-H_mix(v) }.

The maximum includes i=star. This is the explicit finite interpolation
construction of accepted fact 1252b8823bb5a290, proof section 2, applied to
the entire finite data set. The checked Q inequalities imply that f_mix
interpolates every (X_i,G_i,F_i), is convex differentiable and 1-smooth,
and has f_mix(0)=0=min f_mix. Thus the mixed data are one actual GD
trajectory of one fixed function; they are not an adaptive oracle or a
reset of the function at a bridge.

## 4. A universal quantitative two-cut necessary condition

Any primitive h as above necessarily satisfies

    r_L r_R [A^2+r_L(T_tot+A)] <= A^2 BC.           (8)

First assume r_L r_R<BC and choose epsilon_mix=epsilon_max in (6).
Using D_tail=B+C+r_R, substitution into (3)-(5) gives

    V_mix = (BC+r_R D_tail)(D_tail+r_L)
              /[D_tail^2 r_R(BC-r_L r_R)]
             * {A^2 BC-r_L r_R[A^2+r_L(T_tot+A)]}.

The prefactor is positive, proving necessity of (8) in this case. For an
algebra check, before the final factorization the numerator is

    (BC+r_R D_tail)
       {A^2[BC(D_tail+r_L)-r_L r_R D_tail]
                                     -T_tot^2 r_L^2 r_R}.

Use A^2 D_tail+T_tot^2 r_L
=(D_tail+r_L)[A^2+r_L(T_tot+A)] to obtain the displayed factorization.

If r_L r_R>BC, set z_aux=-p_aux=B/r_L and beta_inner>z_aux, and use (7).
Equation (5) becomes

    V_mix=(beta_inner+eta_cut z_aux)/(beta_inner-z_aux)
             * {A^2-T_tot^2[(1+eta_cut)beta_inner/z_aux-eta_cut]}.

The bracket is strictly smaller than A^2-T_tot^2<0. Hence no such schedule
is primitive. If r_L r_R=BC, V_aux=z_aux^2(A^2-T_tot^2)<0, so sufficiently
large epsilon_mix in the fully legal mixed data again gives V_mix<0.
This excludes the two remaining cases and completes (8).

No quadratic-balance assumption about a,b,c appears in this argument.

## 5. Saturated first cut forces its inner tail cut

Suppose in addition r_L T_tot=A D_tail. Then eta_cut=A/T_tot, V_base=0,
and A^2+r_L(T_tot+A)=A T_tot. Condition (8) reduces to

    T_tot r_L r_R<=ABC,
    equivalently r_R D_tail<=BC.                   (9)

Therefore a positive defect r_R D_tail>BC in the inner tail cannot be
repaired by any signed storage or full collection of interpolation edges
while keeping this outer cut exactly saturated. This statement concerns
primitive validity of this actual schedule, not all objective certificates.

The geometry also explains the conclusion without (8): at outer saturation
(4) becomes (T_tot/D_tail)^2[B^2-D_tail^2 beta_inner^2], which is strictly
negative exactly when the tail cut fails. Any sufficiently small positive
mixture allowed above then has V_mix<0.

## 6. Explicit refutation candidate for the outstanding eight-step seed

Set u=10/7, C=27/7, A=B=4, and

    D_tail=(165+sqrt(65641))/42,
    r_R=D_tail-55/7,
    T_tot=(4+D_tail+sqrt((4+D_tail)^2+16D_tail))/2,
    r_L=T_tot-4-D_tail.

The schedule is

    (3/2,3/2,1+r_L,3/2,3/2,1+r_R,10/7,10/7).

Directly from these root equations,

    r_R D_tail=196/9, r_L T_tot=4D_tail,
    BC=108/7<196/9.

Thus (9) fails. Here is a concrete mixing scale without an unspecified
smallness parameter. Define eta_cut=r_L/D_tail, beta_inner=r_R/C,
p_aux=-4/r_L, and

    epsilon_mix=eta_cut(1+eta_cut)
                      /[2 beta_inner(-p_aux-beta_inner)].          (10)

It is positive: the first defining polynomial has its positive root in
(10,101/10), and substituting 5/2 into
r_L^2+(4+D_tail)r_L-4D_tail shows r_L<5/2. Hence
r_L r_R<(5/2)(157/70)=157/28<108/7=BC. Formula (10) is half of (6).

For reference the two position arrays are

    base: (4,5/2,1,-r_L,-r_L+(3/2)eta_cut,
           -r_L+3eta_cut,-C eta_cut,-(1+u)eta_cut,-eta_cut),
    aux:  (4p_aux,(5/2)p_aux,p_aux,4,5/2,1,
           -r_R,-(1+u)beta_inner,-beta_inner).

The gradient arrays are

    base: (1,1,1,-eta_cut,-eta_cut,-eta_cut,
                           -eta_cut,-eta_cut,-eta_cut),
    aux:  (p_aux,p_aux,p_aux,1,1,1,
                           -beta_inner,-beta_inner,-beta_inner).

Values are g_i x_i-g_i^2/2 in each coordinate. Sections 2-3 show that
their mixed two-dimensional jets come from the explicit fixed f_mix.
Finally beta_inner D_tail=1372/243=4(343/243), so

    V_mix = epsilon_mix(T_tot/D_tail)^2
                  [16-(1372/243)^2]
          = -epsilon_mix(T_tot/D_tail)^2 * 937600/59049 < 0.        (11)

This gives an exact concrete primitive counterexample for the proposed
eight-step seed. It closes that seed's proposed primitive amplification.
It makes no claim that a different direct objective certificate is
impossible, and does not settle the unrestricted asymptotic target.

## Literature and verification status

Targeted Matlas and web retrieval supplied no theorem used in this proof.
The primitive/Huber regime had already been audited in previous rounds;
this continuation uses the accepted finite interpolation construction
rather than an external black box. All new results above remain candidates
pending a selected verifier allocation. No fact was submitted or written.

claim: C20 refutes the wider independent-secant envelope: on H_m, choosing lambda_t=1/4 for h_t<=1 and lambda_t=1 for h_t>1 yields relaxed radius >=exp(2^(m-18)/20) for every m>=23. evidence:
# The factor-four sector relaxation grows, but its transcript is not legal

Status: complete unverified counterexample to an extension of the relaxed
product bound. This is NOT a counterexample to a scalar GD convergence
claim and is NOT a legal hard function. The fixed-function incompatibility
is proved explicitly below. No verifier call is allocated.

## 1. The precise relaxed claim that fails

Set c=13/5, a=c^(-17), b_j=a c^j, H_0=(), and
H_(j+1)=(H_j,b_j,H_j). Consider the relaxed scalar recurrence

    x_(t+1)=(1-h_t lambda_t)x_t,    x_0=1,

with independently selectable lambda_t in [1/4,1]. Use the deterministic
rule

    lambda_t=1/4 when h_t<=1,
    lambda_t=1   when h_t>1.                              (1)

On the discrete step levels in H_m, this attains every factor of
q_4(h)=max(1-h/4,h-1): the branch switch is at h=8/5, whereas the two
consecutive schedule levels around it are b_17=1 and b_18=13/5.

For every m>=23 the resulting terminal amplitude satisfies

    |x_(2^m-1)| >= exp[2^(m-18)/20].                      (2)

Thus the uniform damping conclusion for independent secants in a
factor-13/5 band cannot be extended to an arbitrary fixed-width band
without further restrictions. It already fails at width four.

## 2. An exact product lower bound

Define

    p_17=product_(h in H_17)(1-h/4)>0,
    P_4(m)=product_(j=0)^(m-1)q_4(b_j)^(2^(m-j-1)).

The relaxed trajectory has |x_(2^m-1)|=P_4(m). In H_17, every h/4 is at
most 1/(4c)=5/52 and its total is at most (5/3)/4=5/12. The inequality
log(1-u)>=-u/(1-v) for 0<=u<=v<1 follows by integrating -1/(1-z).
Therefore

    log p_17 >= -(52/47)(5/12)=-65/141.                   (3)

For m>=23, divide log P_4(m) by 2^(m-18), retain the levels 17 through
22, and discard only positive higher-level terms. This gives

    log P_4(m)/2^(m-18)
      >= 2 log p_17+log(3/4)
                    +sum_(ell=1)^5 2^(-ell)log(c^ell-1).

Use log(3/4)>=-1/3. For x>=1,

    log x >= 2(x-1)/(x+1),

because the derivative of the difference is
(x-1)^2/[x(x+1)^2]>=0 and its value at 1 is zero. In particular,

    (1/2)log(c-1) >= 3/13,
    (1/4)log(c^2-1)=(1/2)log(12/5) >= 7/17,
    (1/8)log(c^3-1) > (1/8)log 16 >= 1/3,
    (1/16)log(c^4-1) > (1/16)log 32 >= 5/24,
    (1/32)log(c^5-1) > (1/32)log 64 >= 1/8.

The last three use log 2>=2/3 and the direct rational comparisons
c^3-1>16, c^4-1>32, c^5-1>64. Consequently

    log P_4(m)/2^(m-18)
      > -130/141+3/13+7/17+1/3
      > -9/13+7/17+1/3
       =35/663 >1/20.                                   (4)

Here 130/141<12/13. Equation (4) proves (2) with room to spare.
This is an analytic calculation, not a numerical sweep.

## 3. Why the maximizing transcript cannot be a fixed convex function

Let t be the query index of the first step b_18=13/5 in H_m, m>=19.
All preceding steps belong to H_18 and have size at most one. Under (1)
all preceding lambda values are 1/4, all preceding iterates are positive,
and the immediately preceding step has size a. Write X=x_(t-1)>0.

The requested data at the two adjacent queries would be

    x_(t-1)=X,                  g_(t-1)=X/4,
    x_t=(1-a/4)X,               g_t=x_t.

Since 0<a<1,

    0<x_t<X,          g_t>(3/4)X>X/4=g_(t-1).

A nondecreasing derivative must instead satisfy g_t<=g_(t-1). The
proposed data violate monotonicity before the first large step has even
been taken. Thus no single differentiable convex scalar function can
produce this transcript. Its growing amplitude cannot be advertised as
an objective lower bound, a legal scalar counterexample, or a solution
to the multiscale construction task.

## 4. A necessary local repair, not a sufficient full-history condition

For any legitimate scalar convex function with 1-Lipschitz derivative and
minimum at zero, take a nonzero query x with secant lambda=g(x)/x>0.
For a step 0<=h<=1 with h lambda<1, let x'=x-hg(x), and let
lambda'=g(x')/x'. Then x' stays on the same ray and

    (1-h)|g(x)| <= |g(x')| <= |g(x)|,

by monotonicity and the 1-Lipschitz bound. Dividing by
|x'|=(1-h lambda)|x| proves the exact necessary interval

    lambda(1-h)/(1-h lambda)
        <= lambda' <= lambda/(1-h lambda).              (5)

For the preceding small step h=a and lambda=1/4, (5) requires
lambda'<=1/(4-a)<1, immediately rejecting (1).

A general state recursion must retain at least this gradient/position
compatibility, in addition to the sign and secant band. It must also retain
compatibility at nonadjacent revisits to a previously traversed interval;
(5) alone does not establish interpolation by one fixed function. The
factor-four relaxed route is closed, while the actual broad scalar class
remains unresolved.

# A two-dimensional exact counterexample to the asymmetric eight-step seed

Status: complete UNVERIFIED counterexample, worker max, 2026-09-26.
No verifier or numerical solver call. This attacks the precise schedule
in finding 29a1f4a5269032b1, not a generic three-block rule and not the
unrestricted minimax target. Every needed calculation is included below.

## 1. Exact candidate and elementary parameter bounds

Define

    u=10/7, C=1+2u=27/7,
    D=(165+sqrt(65641))/42,
    s=D-55/7,
    T=(4+D+sqrt((4+D)^2+16D))/2,
    r=T-4-D.

The actual prescribed schedule is

    h=(3/2,3/2,1+r,3/2,3/2,1+s,10/7,10/7).           (1)

Its physical capacity is T=1+sum h_i=83/7+r+s. Directly from the
two quadratic equations,

    D s=196/9, rT=4D, Trs=784/9.                       (2)

For later exact estimates,

    10<D<21/2, 12/5<r<5/2, 0<s<98/45.                 (3)

Indeed P(D)=D^2-(55/7)D-196/9 is negative at10, with P(10)=-22/63,
and positive at21/2, with P(21/2)=215/36. Its positive root lies
between those values. The positive root r of
r^2+(4+D)r-4D=0 exceeds12/5 because the polynomial there is
384/25-(8/5)D<0. It is less than5/2 because its value there is
65/4-(3/2)D>1/2. The s bounds follow from (2) and D>10.

Put

    kappa=s/C=7s/27, so 0<kappa<686/1215<3/5,
    v=sqrt((5r-8)/800)>0,
    g_A=(1/4,0),
    g_B=(-1/10,v),
    g_C=-kappa g_B.                                    (4)

In particular

    ||g_B||^2=r/160,
    <g_A,g_B>=-1/40,
    <g_A,g_C>=kappa/40.                                (5)

## 2. One globally fixed function and the actual GD trajectory

On R^2 define, before running GD,

    J(z)=max(0,<g_A,z>,<g_B,z>,<g_C,z>),
    f(x)=min_z[J(z)+||x-z||^2/2].                       (6)

This is one finite convex polyhedral function and its unit Moreau
envelope. The quadratic proximal objective is coercive and strictly
convex, so its minimizer is unique. Subgradient monotonicity gives
||grad f(x)-grad f(y)||^2<=<grad f(x)-grad f(y),x-y>;
the minimizing inequalities identify grad f=x-prox_J(x). Thus f is
globally convex, differentiable, and 1-smooth. It is nonnegative and
minimized at origin. The two gradient directions g_A and g_B are not
collinear because v>0.

Start at x_0=(1,0)=4g_A. The displayed queries and gradients are

    x_0=(1,0),                         grad f(x_0)=g_A,
    x_1=(5/8,0),                       grad f(x_1)=g_A,
    x_2=(1/4,0),                       grad f(x_2)=g_A,
    x_3=(-r/4,0),                      grad f(x_3)=g_B,
    x_4=x_3-(3/2)g_B,                  grad f(x_4)=g_B,
    x_5=x_3-3g_B,                      grad f(x_5)=g_B,
    x_6=x_3-(4+s)g_B,                  grad f(x_6)=g_C,
    x_7=x_6-u g_C,                     grad f(x_7)=g_C,
    x_8=x_6-2u g_C,                    grad f(x_8)=g_C.    (7)

Define the residual point

    Z=x_3-4g_B=(-r/4+2/5,-4v).

From (5), <g_B,Z>=r/40-4r/160=0, hence also <g_C,Z>=0.
Since Ckappa=s and C=1+2u,

    x_6=Z+Cg_C, x_8=Z+g_C.                             (8)

The arithmetic in (7) proves the GD updates for (1); the next paragraph
checks that all these gradients are the actual gradients of (6).

### Every old and future affine plane, on all three blocks

If g is an active plane normal in J at x-g, its subgradient inequality
proves that x-g uniquely minimizes the proximal objective. Therefore
it suffices to compare all four planes there.

On the first pair and its following checkpoint query, write the query
as (4-t)g_A, with ordinary cumulative t in [0,3]. Its proposed
proximal point is d g_A, d=3-t>=0. The current plane has value d/16.
The B plane has value -d/40<=0. The C plane has value d kappa/40,
whose ratio to the current value when d>0 is 2kappa/5<1. The zero
plane is also dominated, including the case d=0. This checks both
future planes at ALL first-block queries.

On the middle pair and its following checkpoint query, write the query
as x_3-tg_B, t in [0,3]. Its proposed proximal point is Z+d g_B,
d=3-t>=0. The current B value is d r/160. The future C value is
-kappa d r/160<=0. The old A value is

    <g_A,Z>+d<g_A,g_B>=-(5r-8)/80-d/40<0.

Thus every plane, including zero, is dominated there too.

On the last pair and at the final point, the proposed proximal point is
Z+d g_C with 0<=d<=C-1=20/7. The selected C value is
d kappa^2 r/160, the B value is its negative multiple -1/kappa,
and zero is dominated. The old A comparison is exactly

    2(5r-8)>=d kappa(4-r kappa).                        (9)

Its left side is greater than8 by (3). If 4-r kappa were negative
the right side would be nonpositive. Otherwise, using (3)--(4), it is
at most

    (20/7)*(3/5)*4=48/7<8.

Hence (9) holds strictly. This checks the potentially harmful positive
correlation with the remote first-block plane. It is the constraint
omitted by a purely scalar block gluing or a quadratic-product test.

All gradients in (7) are therefore actual gradients of the same fixed
function (6). The zero set is nonempty and the true minimum is zero.
Moreover origin is closest to x_0: any minimizing z satisfies
<g_A,z><=0, hence its first coordinate is nonpositive and
||(1,0)-z||^2>=1. The actual initial distance is exactly one.

## 3. Exact negative primitive energy

The proposed saturated primitive inequality, with physical capacity
T=1+sum_(i=0)^7 h_i and S=T-1, requires nonnegativity of

    V_h=2 sum_(i=0)^7 h_i(f_i-f_8)
       +sum_(i=0)^7 h_i(1-h_i)||g_i||^2
       -S T ||g_8||^2,                                (10)

for every convex 1-smooth GD trajectory. This is the precise primitive
energy being tested; no nonsaturated objective certificate is rejected
by merely giving it this name.

Every sampled gradient here is one of the active homogeneous plane
normals, so its actual value satisfies

    f_i=<g_i,x_i>-||g_i||^2/2, including i=8.             (11)

In particular every optimum interpolation residual is zero. Substituting
(11) into (10), and using x_(i+1)=x_i-h_i g_i, gives the complete telescope

    2sum h_i f_i+sum h_i(1-h_i)||g_i||^2
      =sum[2h_i<g_i,x_i>-h_i^2||g_i||^2]
      =||x_0||^2-||x_8||^2,

    V_h=||x_0||^2-||x_8+Sg_8||^2.                      (12)

By (8), g_8=g_C, x_8=Z+g_C and <Z,g_C>=0. A direct calculation gives

    ||Z||^2=r(5r-8)/80,
    T^2||g_C||^2=T^2 r s^2/(160 C^2)
                 =941192/(295245 r),                  (13)

where (2) was used in the second equality. Hence the EXACT energy is

    V_h=1-r(5r-8)/80-941192/(295245 r).                  (14)

This is strictly negative with a rational margin. Since r<5/2,

    T^2||g_C||^2 >1882384/1476225>1,
    V_h < -406159/1476225 <0.                           (15)

The additional term ||Z||^2 is positive and strengthens the rejection.
No numerical residual, optimizer output, or limiting argument is needed.

## 4. Scope

Equations (6)--(15) give a legal two-dimensional counterexample to the
exact eight-step schedule (1) being primitive at its proposed physical
capacity T. It therefore cannot be used as a primitive seed for the
conditional amplification route in that form. Passing all original
single-cut tests and full-curvature equality does not save that seed.

This does not rule out a weaker objective certificate for the same
schedule, different bridge parameters, or any unrestricted minimax
statement. It is a new unverified shared counterexample; no correctness
claim is being promoted into the fact graph without a verifier allocation.

evidence:
# Physical block sum and an endpoint resolvent bound do not close the join

Status: complete unverified counterexample to a proposed induction interface.
No fact_submit request is allocated. This is not a counterexample for Hsc_m.

## Exact claim under test

For a fixed scalar convex1-smooth function f with minimum0, let T_A denote
the actual GD return map of a nonnegative block A with physical step sum S.
The proposed induction summary is

    |T_A(x)|+S|f'(T_A(x))| <= |x| for every real x.       (1)

One might try to close the ruler recursion by deriving the same property
with coefficient2S+b for the joined block (A,b,A), using only(1), the
physical sum S, and monotonicity/smoothness of the same fixed f. That
implication is false at b/S=3/5, including arbitrarily large S. It already
fails on a unit quadratic, even when T_A itself is increasing, nonexpansive,
and sign-preserving and (1) holds with equality for every initial point.

## One fixed function and all five actual GD steps

Fix S>=8, b>=3S/5, and put

    h_minus=(S/2)(1-sqrt((S-3)/(S+1))),
    h_plus =(S/2)(1+sqrt((S-3)/(S+1))),
    A=(h_minus,h_plus).

Both steps are finite and positive. Their sum is exactly S and their
product is S^2/(S+1). Take f(x)=x^2/2, with derivative g(x)=x and valid
minimizer0. Each GD step is x->(1-h)x. Therefore

    T_A(x)=(1-h_minus)(1-h_plus)x=x/(S+1).             (2)

Equation(2) proves (1) with equality for every real x, as well as all the
additional map properties in the preceding paragraph. No gradient data
are chosen at runtime; f is the same unit quadratic throughout.

Starting at1, the five-step schedule (h_minus,h_plus,b,h_minus,h_plus)
has the exact trajectory

    x_0=1,
    x_1=1-h_minus,
    x_2=1/(S+1),
    x_3=(1-b)/(S+1),
    x_4=(1-h_minus)(1-b)/(S+1),
    x_5=(1-b)/(S+1)^2.

Its complete objective is f(x_5)=(b-1)^2/[2(S+1)^4]. The left side of
the claimed joined endpoint bound is

    |x_5|+(2S+b)|g(x_5)|
      =(b-1)(1+2S+b)/(S+1)^2.                         (3)

The numerator minus (S+1)^2 is increasing in b for b>=1. At b=3S/5
it equals

    (14/25)S^2-4S-2,

which is positive at S=8 and strictly increasing for S>=8. Thus (3)>1,
contradicting the claimed conclusion while preserving all stated premises.

For a small exact instance take S=8 and b=24/5. Then

    A=(4-(4/3)sqrt(5),4+(4/3)sqrt(5)),
    x_5=-19/405,
    |x_5|+(104/5)|g(x_5)|=2071/2025>1.

## Exact match to the physical ruler join ratio

For c_sc=13/5, a_sc=c_sc^(-17), the actual ruler prefix Hsc_r has

    S=ssc_r=a_sc(c_sc^r-2^r)/(c_sc-2), b=bsc_r=a_sc c_sc^r.

Hence b/S=(c_sc-2)/(1-(2/c_sc)^r)>3/5. For r>=19, S>=
(13/8)bsc_r>8. The construction above therefore produces a different
two-step block A having exactly the same physical sum S and satisfying
the proposed endpoint summary, for which the join at the actual bridge
bsc_r fails that summary. Merely knowing S and(1) cannot distinguish A
from an induction hypothesis about Hsc_r.

The example does not say Hsc_r has the same return map as A. Indeed A
has its own long internal steps, and the ruler block has essential
internal damping information that(1) discards. The failure rules out only
this endpoint-only implication. It neither refutes(1) for Hsc_r nor
establishes instability or a benchmark-scale objective on Hsc_m.

The weaker pair of bounds |T_A(x)|<=|x| and
|g(T_A(x))|<=|x|/(S+1) also cannot imply the claimed joined summary,
because this same example satisfies both. The open alternative is an
invariant retaining internal chronology or fixed-profile interval data.

Matlas retrieval for the precise composition claim returned unrelated
solver and extra-gradient results. This example is entirely in the
previously audited scalar quadratic regime; no additional external
theorem or literature premise is required.

not the unrestricted all-schedule comparison. Every new calculation used
below is included here; no unverified finding is a premise.

  and the pointwise maximal completion at a genuinely unqueried terminal.
- `dfde2fa326c908bf`: the exact Chebyshev steps, their sum and polynomial,

- `b98bb807d514e80d`: the single-cut functional K_n, the exact benchmark
  recursions, and B_n <= 1+4 n^p for p=log_2(3).

We use smoothness one and initial distance one throughout. Thus the
normalized objective is 2f(x_n). General smoothness follows by scaling.

## 1. An arbitrary-block prefix with a completely specified fresh direction

Let M>=2 and A>=4. Prescribe ANY two nonnegative ordinary lists of sum
M-1 each, separated by the checkpoint AM+1. A final step b will be added
after the second list. Work in R^2 and put

    nu=sqrt(2A-4),
    p=(1,0)/M,                  q=(-2,nu)/M,
    J(z)=max(0,<p,z>,<q,z>),
    f_old=env_1 J,              x_init=(1,0).

The squared boundary gradient is exactly ||q||^2=2A/M^2. The fresh
component of q has squared norm (2A-4)/M^2; it is not dropped from the
state or normalization.

In the first block every gradient is p. To check this, a query after
ordinary partial mass u has proposed proximal point

    z=(1-(u+1)/M,0),       0<=u<=M-1.

Here <p,z>>=0 and <q,z>=-2<p,z>. Thus p is an active subgradient of J.
At the checkpoint query the position is p and its proximal point is 0.
The checkpoint AM+1 sends the trajectory to X=(-A,0).

In the second block every gradient is q. Write t=u+1 in [1,M]. Its
proposed proximal point is X-tq. The current height is

    <q,X-tq>=(2A/M)(1-t/M)>=0.

Its excess over the p-plane is

    <q-p,X-tq>=3A/M-(2A+2)t/M^2 >= (A-2)/M >0.

This checks both other planes at every actual query, even if an
individual ordinary step is very large. The comparisons are affine in
t, and the displayed bounds hold on the whole interval. The old q-plane
was already checked at every first-block query, so both cross directions
and every queried sample belong to the same fixed J.

The envelope justification is elementary: if g is an active-plane
subgradient at z and x=z+g, its subgradient inequality makes z the unique
minimizer of J(w)+||x-w||^2/2. Adding the inequalities for two such
proximal pairs proves

    ||g(x)-g(x')||^2 <= <g(x)-g(x'),x-x'>.

The minimizing inequalities identify g as the derivative of the convex
envelope, which is consequently 1-smooth. All claimed GD updates and
sample values follow from this fixed envelope.

At the last query, just before the final step b, the proximal point and
position are respectively

    y=X-Mq=(2-A,-nu),         x_last=y+q.

One has <q,y>=0, <p,y><0, f_old(x_last)=||q||^2/2. At ALL old
queries the value and gradient are retained in the completion below.

## 2. The exact four-anchor maximal interpolant

Set

    a=1-1/M,       z_A=(a,0),       delta_A=a/M,
    z_B=X-q,
    delta_B=(M-1)||q||^2.

For a retained jet (x,g,f), its proximal point z=x-g and height
delta=f-||g||^2/2 give the conjugate quadratic

    ||v||^2/2 + <z,v> - delta.

This is exactly the quadratic H_j in fact 1252b8823bb5a290 after
expansion. In the first block (z,delta) traces the line segment from
(z_A,delta_A) to (0,0). Both endpoints are actual queried samples. In
the second block it traces the segment from (z_B,delta_B) to (y,0),
again with both endpoints queried. Therefore the maximum of ALL retained
quadratics, including the optimum jet, is exactly

    H(v)=||v||^2/2 + max(0,
                        <z_A,v>-delta_A,
                        <y,v>,
                        <y,v>+(M-1)(<q,v>-||q||^2)).             (1)

No constraint is deleted: intermediate quadratics are convex
combinations of these endpoint quadratics. By the accepted fact,

    F(x)=sup_v [<x,v>-H(v)]                                    (2)

is one fixed finite convex 1-smooth function, preserves every old query,
has F(0)=0=min F, and is the pointwise maximal such interpolant.
It is selected before running the complete prescribed schedule.

The actual closest-minimizer distance stays ONE. The initial jet is

    x_init=(1,0),  g_init=p,  F(x_init)=1/M-1/(2M^2).

For any minimizer z of F, the accepted interpolation inequality between

    0 >= F(x_init)+<p,z-x_init>+||p||^2/2 = <p,z>.

## 9. Exact optimization of the whole homogeneous second-gradient class

The parallel component need not be fixed at -2/M. There is an explicit
optimal choice, and it applies to TWO UNEQUAL prescribed block masses.
This section includes its own prefix, active-set, and optimization proof.

Let the two ordinary sums be M_0-1 and M_1-1, with M_0>1, M_1>=1.
Let the first bridge be A M_0+1 for ANY A>0, and let the final step be
b>=0. Start from (1,0), use p=(1,0)/M_0 in the first block, and for
0<=kappa<=A put

    q_kappa=(-kappa,sqrt(kappa(A-kappa)))/M_1,
    X=(-A,0),
    y=X-M_1 q_kappa.

Then ||q_kappa||^2=A kappa/M_1^2 and <q_kappa,y>=0. This parameter
covers, up to an orthogonal rotation fixing the first coordinate, EVERY
possible q in any finite dimension that satisfies

    <q,X-M_1 q>=0.

Indeed that equation forces q_1=-M_1||q||^2/A<=0. Setting
kappa=-M_1 q_1 gives the displayed norm and fresh squared component
kappa(A-kappa)/M_1^2, which is nonnegative exactly for kappa in [0,A].
Thus the class being optimized is precisely the homogeneous new-plane
class whose second block ends at proximal value zero, with this first
block fixed. It does not include arbitrary affine intercepts or positive
endpoint levels.

All prefixes are legal for J=max(0,<p,z>,<q_kappa,z>). At an old
first-block proximal point the q-plane is a nonpositive multiple of
the p-plane. At a second-block proximal point X-tq_kappa, 1<=t<=M_1,
the q-plane has value

    A kappa/M_1 * (1-t/M_1)>=0,

while its first coordinate -A+t kappa/M_1 is nonpositive. Hence the
p-plane is <=0. These verify every actual old/new comparison. For
kappa=0 the second block is already at a minimizer and has gradient
zero; no strict positivity is presumed at that endpoint.

Let

    c=1/M_0,  a=1-c,  L=A+2a,
    epsilon=(b-1)/M_1,
    d=(kappa,-sqrt(kappa(A-kappa))),
    z_A=(a,0),  e=z_A-y,
    D=(A-kappa)L+a^2.

For epsilon>=0 the terminal point is y+epsilon d. The complete retained
conjugate maximum is again exactly four terms:

    H_kappa(v)=||v||^2/2+max(0,
                   <z_A,v>-ac,
                   <y,v>,
                   <y,v>+(M_1-1)(<q_kappa,v>-||q_kappa||^2)). (20)

For M_1=1 the last term duplicates the preceding term. The endpoint
data produce (20) directly: first-block proximal heights are <p,z>,
and second-block proximal heights are <q_kappa,z>. All intermediate
quadratics are convex combinations of the two endpoints of their own
block. Accepted fact 1252b8823bb5a290 gives the fixed maximal interpolant
F_kappa=H_kappa^*. The initial-jet inequality <p,z><=0 at every
minimizer proves the actual closest distance is one, for every kappa.

Define clip_[0,1](u)=max(0,min(1,u)), and put

    tau=clip_[0,1](a(kappa epsilon-c)/D),
    v=epsilon d-tau e.                                      (21)

Here D>=a^2>0. The useful identities are

    ||d||^2=A kappa,    <d,e>=a kappa,
    <y,d>=0,           <y,e>=-(A-kappa)(A+a)<=0.              (22)

If tau=0, then kappa epsilon<=c, the y-term and zero term tie,
and the z_A-term is <=0. If 0<tau<1, the y-term and z_A-term tie,
since <e,v>=ac, and the y-term is >=0. If tau=1, then
<e,v>>=ac, so the z_A-term dominates the y-term. It is also >=0:
the inequality a(kappa epsilon-c)>=D implies

    v_1=-(A-kappa)+kappa epsilon-a
        >= (A-kappa)(A/a+1)+c >= c.

For 0<kappa<=A, the fourth term never exceeds the y-term. In the
interior case,

    <q_kappa,v>=-kappa(A epsilon-a tau)/M_1<=0,

because a tau<=a^2 kappa epsilon/D<=A epsilon; the last inequality
uses a^2 kappa<=A D. For tau=0 it is immediate. For tau=1, the
condition above gives kappa epsilon>=D/a+c>=a+c=1, hence
A epsilon>=1>a. At kappa=0 this fourth term simply equals the y-term.

For 0<tau<1, y+tau e is an active convex combination of slopes;
at tau=0 or1 the appropriate endpoint is active. Since
x_n=v+y+tau e, this proves the exact terminal gradient and value for
EVERY kappa and EVERY epsilon>=0. The value is

    V_kappa = min_(0<=t<=1) J_kappa(t),
    J_kappa(t)=A kappa epsilon^2
               -2t a(kappa epsilon-c)
               +t^2[(A-kappa)L+a^2].                        (23)

This also proves that V_kappa is concave in kappa: it is a minimum of
affine functions of kappa. There is no numerical or existence step in
the following optimization.

### Exact global optimizer in kappa

Set

    epsilon_low=L/[A M_0(A+a)],
    epsilon_high=L/A.

When epsilon_low<epsilon<epsilon_high, choose

    kappa_opt=A(A+a)/L + a/[M_0 epsilon(A+a)],
    tau_opt=epsilon A/L.                                    (24)

These inequalities ensure 0<kappa_opt<A and 0<tau_opt<1. This is the
global optimizer over the ENTIRE kappa interval. To prove it, fix
t=tau_opt in (23). The coefficient of kappa is

    A epsilon^2-2a epsilon t-L t^2=0.

Consequently (23) bounds every V_kappa by the SAME number

    V_opt=epsilon^2 [A(A+a)/L]^2 + 2epsilon Aac/L.             (25)

Substitution of (24) in the unconstrained minimizer of (23) gives
exactly tau_opt, so this bound is attained. The argument is an explicit
upper certificate on this parameter class, paired with its displayed
realizing direction; it assumes no minimax interchange.

Outside that open epsilon interval, kappa_opt=A is a global optimizer.
Here is a direct proof including cases when the interval is empty.
At kappa=A let

    t_A=clip_[0,1]((A epsilon-c)/a).

If epsilon<=epsilon_low, then t_A<=epsilon A/L. If
epsilon>=epsilon_high, then t_A<=1<=epsilon A/L. In either case the
coefficient A epsilon^2-2a epsilon t_A-L t_A^2 of kappa in
J_kappa(t_A) is nonnegative. For 0<=kappa<=A it follows that

    V_kappa<=J_kappa(t_A)<=J_A(t_A)=V_A.

Thus the endpoint A attains the global maximum, and both transition
equalities cause no loss. If epsilon_low>=epsilon_high, these two
outside ranges cover every epsilon>=0 and no interior case exists.

For this scalar endpoint write x=A epsilon. Its exact value is

    V_A=x^2,                   0<=x<=c,
        2cx-c^2,               c<=x<=1,
        (x-a)^2+2ac,           x>=1.                          (26)

This follows either from (23) or directly from the three possible
clipped values of t_A. Formulas (24)-(26) are a complete constructive
solution for every finite b>=1, unequal M_0,M_1, and A>0.

If 0<=b<=1, the final point lies on the segment from y+q_kappa to y.
Every retained interpolant has F(y)=0 and gradient zero there, and has
gradient q_kappa and value ||q_kappa||^2/2 at y+q_kappa. The unit
Lipschitz bound and the triangle inequality force gradient t q_kappa
at y+t q_kappa for 0<=t<=1: the distances to gradients 0 and q_kappa
are at most t||q_kappa|| and (1-t)||q_kappa||, whose sum is their
mutual distance. Equality forces the collinear point. Integrating
gives the exact final value

    (1-b)^2 A kappa/M_1^2.

It is maximized by kappa=A. This handles zero final steps and b=1.

For the remaining degenerate first mass M_0=1, its sole nonzero
initial jet has gradient (1,0) and proximal point zero. Taking kappa=A
makes y=0 and reduces the maximal terminal function on the positive
axis to x^2/2, because every negative-side retained conjugate affine
term is nonpositive there. It attains A^2(b-1)^2/M_1^2 for b>=1.
For any kappa the forced minimizer y and smoothness bound give the
upper bound A kappa(b-1)^2/M_1^2, proving optimality. The b<=1
segment proof gives the same formula. Thus M_0=1 needs no division
by a or omitted limiting argument.

### Quantitative improvement on the same full-horizon family

In (7) take M_0=M_1=M, A=M^(1/12), epsilon=M^(-1/3). The strict
interior regime applies: epsilon<1<epsilon_high, and

    epsilon_low <= (A+2)/(A^2 M) <= 2/(AM) < epsilon

for A>=4 and M>=4^12. Hence (24) is an explicit legal direction on
EXACTLY THE SAME schedules, and its error is (25). Since
(A+a)/(A+2a)>=5/6 for A>=4 and 0<a<=1,

    V_opt >= (25/36) A^2 epsilon^2 >= (1/2) M^(-1/2).         (27)

This exceeds the earlier bound M^(-7/12) by at least A/2, which
tends to infinity. All bounds (11)-(17) on the actual schedules stay
unchanged. In particular (27) exceeds 1/B_n at every n>=24578,
while the three baseline ratios still tend to zero. Against every
scalar continuation in Section8 its gain is at least M^(1/3)/4.

The uncompleted envelope still has terminal value zero. Indeed, for
these parameters A epsilon=M^(-1/4)<=1/64 and a>=1/2. Also

    A-kappa_opt = Aa/(A+2a)-a/[M epsilon(A+a)] >= a/2,

using A/(A+2a)>=2/3 and 1/[M epsilon(A+a)]<=M^(-3/4)<=1/6.
Thus epsilon kappa_opt<=A epsilon<=a/2<=A-kappa_opt. Both old
planes are nonpositive at the terminal point. This checks the claimed
completion effect after optimizing the angle, rather than inferring
it from the earlier fixed-angle example.

For an arbitrary supplied schedule, each choice of an earlier checkpoint
b_0>1 and its final step determines M_0,M_1,A=(b_0-1)/M_0. Equations
(24)-(26), the b<=1 formula, and the M_0=1 case therefore give a
concrete two-checkpoint lower bound whenever those blocks exhaust the
schedule. Maximizing over the finitely many possible earlier checkpoints
is another valid lower-bound functional; the formulas fully solve its
continuous direction parameter. No comparison with B_n for every
schedule is claimed. In particular, this zero-level second-block class
has value zero when the final step is exactly one. Positive endpoint
levels or a different prefix remain necessary for that part of the
all-schedule problem.

## 10. The unit-final-step obstruction survives positive levels and offsets

The zero value at b=1 in Section9 is not repaired at the benchmark scale
merely by allowing a positive second-block proximal level. A bound for
the ENTIRE constant-second-gradient class is available without choosing
an envelope representation.

Let an arbitrary convex 1-smooth f have minimum zero at the origin. Let
the start of its last ordinary block be X, let that block have sum M_1-1,
and suppose its gradient is the same vector q at every actual sample in
that block, including its last query. Append a unit final step. Its last
queried position is x_E=X-(M_1-1)q. Interpolation with the optimum and
the unit-step descent inequality give, respectively,

    f(x_E)<=<q,x_E>-||q||^2/2,
    f(x_E-q)<=f(x_E)-||q||^2/2.

Consequently

    2f(x_E-q) <=2<q,X>-2M_1||q||^2
       = ||X||^2/(2M_1)-2M_1||q-X/(2M_1)||^2
       <= ||X||^2/(2M_1).                                   (28)

This holds in every dimension, with arbitrary positive values, arbitrary
affine intercepts in any realizing envelope, and arbitrary behavior
away from the retained samples. The constant-gradient hypothesis is
the only special restriction on the final ordinary block.

For the first-block geometry of Section9, X=(-A,0), and all retained
first jets ensure the true closest initial distance is one. The single
cut at the preceding checkpoint AM_0+1, on the same schedule ending in
a unit step, already gives exactly

    K_cut=A^2/(2M_1+1).

Equation (28) is only a factor 1+1/(2M_1) larger. Thus this whole class,
even after freeing every second-block level, direction, intercept and
the maximal terminal completion, cannot beat that baseline by a growing
factor when the final step is one. On the modified schedules (7) with
the last step replaced by one, its bound is M^(-5/6)/2=o(1/B_n), using
the same exact benchmark upper estimate as in (15).

This closes only the proposed extension by positive levels INSIDE a
constant-gradient last block. It leaves varying gradients inside that
block, more chronological cells, and the unrestricted worst case open.
It identifies a precise missing mechanism for extending the new
terminal gain to arbitrary schedules.

## 11. A new universally valid terminal two-checkpoint functional

There is a simple schedule-level consequence, without any parameter
feasibility assumption. In Section9, for M_0>1, fix the direction

    kappa_0=A(A+a)/(A+2a),

independently of the final step. For every epsilon>=0, (23) and ac>=0
give

    V_(kappa_0)
       >= min_(t in R) [A kappa_0 epsilon^2
                        -2t a kappa_0 epsilon+t^2 D_0],
    D_0=a(A+a).

Completing this scalar square yields

    V_(kappa_0) >= kappa_0^2 epsilon^2.                       (29)

Specifically, A kappa_0-a^2 kappa_0^2/D_0=kappa_0^2. The relaxation
to real t and omission of the nonnegative term go in the lower-bound
direction. M_0=1 has the same conclusion with kappa_0=A by its explicit
scalar construction in Section9.

Now let h be ANY finite nonnegative schedule of length n>=2. For an
index j<n-1 with h_j>1 set

    P_j=sum_(t<j) h_t,
    S_j=sum_(j<t<n-1) h_t,
    gamma_j=(h_j-1+P_j)/(h_j-1+2P_j),
    D_j^two=gamma_j^2 *
       [(h_j-1)(h_(n-1)-1)_+/((1+P_j)(1+S_j))]^2.            (30)

Define D_n^two(h) as the maximum of these terms, or zero if there is
no such index (also set it to zero for n<2). Every denominator for an
included j is positive; no 0/0 convention is hidden.

For h_(n-1)>1 apply the actual two-block construction with
M_0=1+P_j, M_1=1+S_j, A=(h_j-1)/M_0 and
epsilon=(h_(n-1)-1)/M_1. All intervening ordinary entries are used
exactly in their prescribed order. Formula (29), with the genuine
normalization one, becomes (30). If h_(n-1)<=1 the displayed term is
zero and the bound holds directly. Thus

    W_n(h) >= max(K_n(h),D_n^two(h))                           (31)

for every nonnegative schedule. The finite maximization over j is part
of adversary selection; it changes no function during a trajectory.
Since 1/2<=gamma_j<=1, a weaker bound replaces gamma_j^2 by 1/4.
This is a new chronological product term, not a putative equality for W.

For the schedules (7), select the large bridge between the two L_N
blocks. Formula (30) gives

    D_n^two(h^[n]) >= (25/36) M^(-1/2),                       (32)

using A>=4 and gamma_j=(A+a)/(A+2a)>=5/6. Thus the improvement over
the previously available K, quadratic, and universal-lens channels is
already visible in an explicit universally valid scalar functional of
the schedule. No optimization oracle is needed to evaluate (30).

## 12. A counterexample to uniform comparison by the enlarged functional

The new functional (31) STILL does not solve the target. This can be
tested constructively without making any claim about small true W.

Keep N,M,A from (7). Let L_N^up be the three increasing copies of
Chi_N and L_N^down the three decreasing copies. Define

    h_bad^(N)=(L_N^up, AM+1, L_N^down, 1).                    (33)

Its length is still 6N+2; the same beginning-zero padding covers every
large integer horizon. All of its D_j^two terms are zero because its
last step is one. Quadratic polynomials are independent of the order
inside each ordinary block. The bound (10) still applies, with the
smaller final factor 1+lambda instead of 1+b lambda; the same is true
of (13)-(14). Thus the quadratic and universal-lens channels are again
O(M^(-5/6)).

Here every single-cut term is small as well. The first increasing block
has the same bound 81/(2AM) as before. At the bridge the exact term is
A^2/(2M+1). For a cut in the DECREASING block, denote by T_j its full
tail mass. Within a decreasing copy, each entry is at most four times
its successor, by the adjacent-ratio proof in Section5. A last entry
in a copy is <=4/3; it is either followed by another copy or by the
unit final step. Hence every entry in the second block obeys

    h_j <=4(1+T_j),       h_j<=M.

The full prefix mass there is at least (A+1)M. Its single-cut term is
therefore at most

    h_j^2/[A^2 M^2(1+2T_j)] <=4/(A^2 M).

The final unit-step cut contributes zero, and the global Huber term
is <=1/M. Consequently K_n(h_bad^[n])<=41M^(-5/6), and the same
exact-B_n estimate (15) proves

    max(K_n(h_bad^[n]),D_n^two(h_bad^[n]),Q_n(h_bad^[n]),
        sup_(z in Lens_n) Gap_(h_bad^[n])(z)) / U_n^ZJ ->0.    (34)

This is an explicit refutation of the proposed UNIFORM comparison by
that combined lower functional. It is not a counterexample to the
unrestricted target and not an upper bound on W_n(h_bad^[n]). The
unit-tail cap (28) additionally shows that allowing arbitrary positive
levels in one constant-gradient second block cannot repair this
failure. A repair must use internal gradient changes, more cells, or a
different source of retained terminal value.

## Scope and remaining task

This joint proof supplies an exact arbitrary-block terminal policy, a
four-anchor active-set formula, all old/new comparisons, the actual
boundary gradient, true distance normalization, and a quantitative
family at every large horizon that defeats several baseline channels.
It does not assert that every schedule has an advantageous two-block
partition, that the completed function remains adverse after an
arbitrary further suffix, or that a greedy intermediate completion is
globally optimal. The all-schedule exact-profile comparison remains open.

Targeted Matlas searches returned no external theorem used in the proof.
The exact accepted predecessors above were read. A search hit for an
older lower-bound paper returned HTTP 503 and was not relied on. All
new results remain candidates because the current assignment allocates
no additional verifier requests.

evidence:
# Projection capacity calibration and an exponential false-positive family

Status: complete candidate calculations, NOT verifier-accepted. No solver or
fact_submit. All new ingredients are proved below. Accepted fact
1252b8823bb5a290 supplies the smooth-convex interpolation inequalities;
b98bb807d514e80d supplies only the named exact benchmark recursion.
This is a capacity test, not a proof of the all-length capacity conjecture.

For a nonnegative schedule h of length n, put S=sum h_i, D=1+S, and

    V_h=2sum_(i<n)h_i(f_i-f_n)
       +sum_(i<n)h_i(1-h_i)||g_i||^2-SD||g_n||^2.

Primitive means V_h>=0 on every actual convex differentiable 1-smooth
GD run. All witnesses and certificates below use the physical steps.

## 1. Exact projection witnesses give two necessary tests

For any compact interval C containing zero, the function
F_C(x)=max_(v in C)(xv-v^2/2) is convex, differentiable and 1-smooth,
with derivative equal to the nearest-point projection onto C. This follows
by completing the square; the projection normal inequality gives its
1-Lipschitz property. At every actual sample, f_i=x_i g_i-g_i^2/2.
The squared-distance telescope therefore gives exactly

    V_h=x_0^2-(x_n+Sg_n)^2.                           (1)

Choose one checkpoint b=h_j>1. Put
A=1+sum_(i<j)h_i, B=1+sum_(i>j)h_i, so D=A+B+b-1.
Choose u>0, v=(b-1)u/B, C=[-v,u], and x_0=A u.
Every preceding ordinary step stays on the positive plateau, with
gradient u, and the checkpoint input is exactly u. Its output is
-(b-1)u=-Bv. Every following ordinary step stays on the negative plateau,
with gradient -v, and the final point is -v. All function values are
those of the ONE fixed projection function, so (1) gives

    V_h=A^2u^2-D^2(b-1)^2u^2/B^2.

Thus every primitive schedule satisfies the exact cut conditions

    D(h_j-1)_+ <= (1+sum_(i<j)h_i)(1+sum_(i>j)h_i).   (2)

There is a second projection witness: start the scalar unit quadratic
at1 and let x_i=product_(t<i)(1-h_t). A compact interval containing zero
and ALL these finitely many points has projection gradient g_i=x_i at
every sample and the same values x_i^2/2. Therefore every primitive h has

    D |product_(i<n)(1-h_i)| <=1.                    (3)

Condition (3) tests curvature1 only, not all curvatures.

## 2. Exact two-step capacity upper bound

For any primitive h=(h_0,h_1), (2) gives

    h_0,h_1 <= M_D:=2D/(D+1),  D=1+h_0+h_1.          (4)

If a step is at most1 this is automatic; otherwise rearrange its own
cut inequality D(h_i-1)<=D-h_i.
Let D_two be the unique root larger than4 of

    D_two^4-4D_two^3-1=0.                            (5)

We claim D<=D_two. There is nothing to prove if D<4. For D>=4,
(4) and h_0+h_1=D-1 imply both steps lie in
[L_D,M_D], where L_D=D-1-M_D>1. The function
(x-1)(D-2-x) is concave and has the same value at these two endpoints.
Consequently

    (h_0-1)(h_1-1)
      >= (M_D-1)(L_D-1)
      = (D-1)(D^2-3D-2)/(D+1)^2.

Multiplying by D and applying (3) yields

    D(D-1)(D^2-3D-2)<=(D+1)^2,

which is precisely D^4-4D^3-1<=0. The polynomial is strictly increasing
for D>3, negative at4 and positive at5, proving (5)'s uniqueness and
the claimed upper bound.

## 3. An explicit full certificate attains that bound

Put b=sqrt(2) and let a be the positive root of

    a^2+ba=2+2b,
    a=(-b+sqrt(10+8b))/2.

Then 1<a<2. Set S=a+b and L_cert=S(2-b)>0. On the two-step schedule
(a,b), use Q_ij=f_i-f_j+<g_i,x_j-x_i>+||g_i-g_j||^2/2. The following
is an identity on the FULL formal three-gradient space:

    V_(a,b) = sum_(i!=j) lambda_ij (-Q_ij),          (6)

where

    lambda_01=0,
    lambda_10=b L_cert,
    lambda_02=(a-1)L_cert,
    lambda_20=L_cert,
    lambda_21=S(S+b),
    lambda_12=(b-1)lambda_21+b L_cert.

All coefficients are nonnegative, so accepted interpolation necessity
Q_ij<=0 proves primitive validity in every finite dimension.

Here is a full coefficient check. Write u=g_0,v=g_1,w=g_2 and use
x_1=x_0-a u, x_2=x_0-a u-b v. The five residuals used in (6) are

    Q_10=f_1-f_0+(||u||^2+||v||^2)/2+(a-1)<u,v>,
    Q_02=f_0-f_2+(1/2-a)||u||^2+||w||^2/2
                                      -b<u,v>-<u,w>,
    Q_20=f_2-f_0+(||u||^2+||w||^2)/2
                                      +(a-1)<u,w>+b<v,w>,
    Q_12=f_1-f_2+(1/2-b)||v||^2+||w||^2/2-<v,w>,
    Q_21=f_2-f_1+(||v||^2+||w||^2)/2+(b-1)<v,w>.

The three mixed-gradient coefficients cancel directly from the displayed
lambdas. The function coefficients are 2a,2b,-2S: use
(b+2-a)L_cert=2a and (2-b)S(S-b)=2b, both consequences of
aS=2+2b and b^2=2. The squared-gradient coefficients are

    ||u||^2: (a-1)^2 L_cert-a=a(1-a),
    ||v||^2: (2-3b/2)S(S+b)+b(b-1)L_cert=b(1-b),
    ||w||^2: -[aL_cert+bS(S+b)+bL_cert]/2=-S(S+1).

For the first equality, expanding (a-1)^2 S(2-b) using aS=2+2b
gives 2a-a^2. For the second, divide by S; the constant terms cancel
and the result is a(2-3b/2), whose product with S is b-2=b(1-b).
The third uses b^2=2. This verifies every coefficient in (6).

Let D=1+a+b. Then D(a-1)=1+b and
D(a-1)(b-1)=b^2-1=1. Also a=2D/(D+1), so equality holds throughout
the bound in section2. Finally a>3-b because the defining polynomial
at 3-b equals 7-5sqrt(2)<0. Thus D>4 and D=D_two. Explicitly,

    D_two=[2+sqrt(2)+sqrt(10+8sqrt(2))]/2
         =Omega(1,1+sqrt(2)).                        (7)

The last expression uses the exact primitive join notation from
accepted fact b98bb807d514e80d. Equations (2)--(7) give an analytic
capacity bound and an attaining universal certificate, not an SDP result.
This is a two-step calibration, not a new all-length capacity claim.

## 4. Cut tests plus curvature1 admit exponentially large false positives

Fix r_geom=3/2. For each integer k>=1 put

    u_i=(r_geom-1)r_geom^i=(1/2)(3/2)^i, 0<=i<k,
    h^(k)=(u_0,u_1,...,u_(k-1),1,u_(k-1),...,u_1,u_0).

Its length is n=2k+1 and its exact physical capacity is

    D=1+sum h^(k)=2 r_geom^k.                         (8)

Every cut condition (2) holds STRICTLY. For a left-half step, put
A=r_geom^i, b=(r_geom-1)A. The other mass is B=D-r_geom A+1.
Since A<=r_geom^(k-1)=D/(2r_geom),

    AB-D(b-1)
      =D[(2-r_geom)A+1]-r_geom A^2+A
      >=D[(3/2-r_geom)A+1]+A=D+A>0.

The mirror cut has the same two masses interchanged. The center step1
has zero left side in (2); steps below1 also satisfy it trivially.
Condition (3) holds with product ZERO because of that center step.

Nevertheless these schedules are not primitive for every k>=15. This
can be shown on the ONE fixed scalar quadratic f(x)=x^2/4, starting at1.
Its curvature is lambda=1/2, and its final iterate is

    x_n=(1/2)[product_(i=0)^(k-1)(1-r_geom^i/4)]^2.    (9)

None of these factors is zero. For i=0,...,5 the product of their
absolute values is exactly

    C_6=(3/4)(5/8)(7/16)(5/32)(17/64)(115/128)
       =1026375/134217728 > 1/256.

For i>=6, r_geom^i/4>=729/256>2, so

    |1-r_geom^i/4|>=r_geom^i/8>=729/512>sqrt(2),

where the last strict comparison is 729^2>2*512^2. Hence for k>=6,

    x_n > (1/2)(1/256)^2 2^(k-6)=2^(k-23),
    D |g_n|=r_geom^k x_n > 3^k/2^23.                 (10)

For k>=15 this exceeds1, since 3^15=14348907>8388608=2^23.

To check that (10) really forces primitive failure, for any legal
smooth-convex data with minimizer0 put
I_i=<g_i,x_i>-f_i-||g_i||^2/2>=0. A direct telescope gives

    V_h=||x_0||^2-||x_n||^2-2sum h_i I_i
                         -2S f_n-S(S+1)||g_n||^2.

Smoothness and convexity give ||x_n||>=||g_n|| and
2f_n>=||g_n||^2. Thus

    V_h<=||x_0||^2-D^2||g_n||^2.                     (11)

Equation (10) makes (11) negative for the explicit quadratic run.
All steps and function values are actual; the failure is not a relaxed
gradient assignment. Capacity (8) grows exponentially with n, so (2)
and (3) alone cannot establish ANY polynomial capacity upper bound.

This refutes only the cut-plus-curvature1 filter. The curvature1/2 test
explicitly detects the family. It makes no insufficiency claim about
the entire quadratic class, and does not propose a primitive schedule
above the silver-power threshold.

## 5. These scalar defects also have finite simplex projection witnesses

For completeness, the negative energy just established can be placed
inside the requested projection class by finite operations, without
using the unverified C27 reduction as a premise. This also explains why
projection witnesses can detect a failure not detected by (2) or (3).

Given this length n schedule and its negative quadratic energy -v_def,
take an auxiliary diagonal quadratic with eigenvalues
theta_l=(l+1)/(2(n+2)), l=0,...,n, started with all coordinates1.
Its n+1 gradients are independent because the polynomials
P_i(z)=product_(t<i)(1-h_t z) have distinct degrees0,...,n; evaluation
at n+1 distinct theta_l, followed by nonzero row scaling theta_l, is
invertible. All distinct auxiliary Q_ij are strictly negative: they
equal minus one half the A_aux(I-A_aux) squared norm of the sample
position difference, and the relevant polynomial difference cannot
vanish at n+1 distinct nodes.

Let E_aux be its finite energy. Add it in orthogonal coordinates with
squared scale epsilon=v_def/[2(v_def+|E_aux|)]. The product function
is an actual 1-smooth convex function, its new energy is at most
-v_def/2, all new gradients are independent, and all finite Q_ij<0.
Rename these mixed jets x_i,g_i,f_i and their positive definite gradient
Gram matrix A_gram. Choose

    f_*=min_i(f_i-||g_i||^2/2)-1,
    r_i=f_*-f_i+<g_i,x_i>-||g_i||^2/2,
    z_*=sum_j(A_gram^(-1)r)_j g_j.

Then X_i=x_i-z_* and F_i=f_i-f_* satisfy
F_i=<g_i,X_i>-||g_i||^2/2. Every finite residual is unchanged and
equals <X_j-g_j,g_i-g_j><0. The comparison with vertex zero is
<X_i-g_i,-g_i>=-(F_i-||g_i||^2/2)<=-1. These are ALL normal
inequalities for C=conv{0,g_0,...,g_n}, proving P_C(X_i)=g_i and
F_C(X_i)=F_i. Translation and the common value shift leave energy
unchanged. Projection onto the gradient span places this simplex
and its trajectory in dimension n+1 with exactly n+2 vertices.

Thus every k>=15 in (8) has an explicit finite simplex projection
counterexample. This construction preserves the negative sign and
retains every queried vertex, but not normalized objective error.

## Scope and the next missing ingredient

The exact two-step optimum and the exponential false-positive family
are quantitative consequences of actual geometric tests. They identify
precisely why extrapolating the two-step cut/product proof cannot work
at arbitrary length. A general capacity argument must use additional
curvatures or additional coupled simplex normal inequalities. No
unproved inequality with silver exponent is used anywhere above.
